intro: You have spent years in this course learning one skill at a time: a twenty-second hand wash, a level cup of flour, a back stitch, a unit price, a food thermometer, a safe crib, a budget built from take-home pay. The capstone asks you to use all of them at once on a single project that you choose, plan, pay for, make, judge and present. It may be a meal for a group or a piece you sew, and it will be yours from the first line of the plan to the last sentence of the presentation.

The first chapter is the plan. You will write a specification that another person could follow, a cost sheet with every ingredient or material at its unit price, a timeline built backwards from the deadline with checkpoints, an equipment list, a safety page with the standard temperatures and rules, and a rubric that says ahead of time what a good result looks like. Every number on those pages is a number you can check.

The second chapter is the doing and the judging. You will run the timeline on production day, record temperatures, times, receipts and photos as you go, serve or finish the piece, and then score it honestly against your own spec and rubric. You will compare plan to actual, name what you would change and why, present the whole project to an audience, and see how the same cycle of plan, cost, produce and evaluate is the daily work of chefs, dietitians, patternmakers, child-care directors and family educators.
bigQuestion: How do you plan, cost, produce and honestly evaluate a real project so that the result is safe, on budget, on time and worth showing?

timeline.t: Fannie Farmer's Boston Cooking-School cookbook standardizes level measurements so recipes can be scaled and costed
The Lake Placid conferences begin, founding home economics as a field that teaches household planning and budgeting
The Pure Food and Drug Act starts federal food regulation in the United States
The Smith-Lever Act creates the Cooperative Extension system that brings nutrition and family programs to communities
The Smith-Hughes Act funds vocational education, including home economics, in public high schools
The National School Lunch Act makes planned, budgeted school meals a federal program
Food-service kitchens adopt written hazard-analysis and critical-control-point plans, the ancestor of the safety page
The Nutrition Facts label appears on packaged food, giving planners standard serving and nutrient data
Home economics is renamed Family and Consumer Sciences, and national standards for the field follow
USDA lowers the safe minimum temperature for whole cuts of pork to 145 °F with a rest, the figures on today's safety page
MyPlate replaces the food pyramid as the guide for balancing a planned menu
You write a spec, a cost sheet, a timeline and a safety page, and produce a project of your own

words.d: a written, measurable description of what the finished product must be
a limit you must work within, such as time, money, tools or skill
a table listing every item a project uses, its unit price, the amount needed and the resulting cost
the price of one unit of an item, found by dividing the package price by the package size
servings needed divided by servings the recipe makes; every ingredient is multiplied by it
money held back in a budget for a price change or a forgotten item
a schedule of every task with its start time, built backwards from the deadline
a set moment where you compare progress to the timeline while there is still time to fix a delay
a posted page of the standard temperatures, times and rules a project depends on
a scoring table whose rows are the things that matter and whose columns describe each level of quality
the numbers, photos and notes recorded during a project as evidence
the difference between a planned figure and the actual one, with a cause you can name

test.q: Which project statement is complete enough to plan from?
choices: I will cook something for my family
I will cook a soup, a main and a dessert for 12 guests on May 9
I will make a nice dinner soon
test.why: A project statement names the product, the scope and the date.

test.q: A student's idea fails the budget test. What is the right move?
choices: Keep the idea and skip the cost sheet
Ask for more money at the register
Shrink the idea until it fits the budget
test.why: Shrinking the scope keeps the project real; the budget is a fixed constraint.

choices: Tomato soup, 1 cup per person, 12 servings
test.why: Cups and servings can be checked with a measuring cup and a count.

test.q: A guest has a tree-nut allergy. Which plan is safe?
choices: Keep tree nuts out of the whole menu and off shared boards and utensils
Serve nuts in a separate bowl
Tell the guest which dish has nuts
Use only a small amount of nuts
test.why: An allergen is a safety hazard, and trace amounts from shared tools can cause a reaction.

test.q: A 3-lb bag of onions costs $2.40 (example). What is the unit price?
A recipe serves 6 and you need 9 servings. A line calls for 2 cups of broth. What is the scaled amount?
test.why: The factor is 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5, and 2 cups × 1.5 = 3 cups.

test.q: Which item is a hidden cost on a meal's cost sheet?
test.why: Small, necessary supplies are the lines most often forgotten.

test.q: Dinner is at 6:30. A dish bakes 50 minutes and rests 10. When does it go in?
test.why: 6:30 minus 10 minutes rest is 6:20, minus 50 minutes baking is 5:30.

test.q: Why does a frozen roast move to the refrigerator days ahead instead of the counter on the day?
choices: Counter thawing leaves the outside in the 40 to 140 °F danger zone for hours
The counter is needed for prep
test.why: Refrigerator thawing keeps the whole roast at or below 40 °F.

test.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for poultry?
test.why: Poultry is safe at 165 °F; ground meats at 160 °F; whole cuts of beef and pork at 145 °F with a rest.

test.q: A grease fire starts in a pan on the stove. What does the safety page say?
choices: Smother it with a lid or baking soda, never water
test.why: Water spreads burning grease; a lid or baking soda cuts off the air.

test.q: Which rubric level is written correctly?
choices: Excellent: seams at 5/8 inch within 1/16 inch, no puckers
Excellent: the student worked hard on the seams
test.why: Rubric levels use numbers or tools so they can be checked the same way by anyone.

test.q: Which record proves the chicken was safe?
choices: A thermometer reading of 165 °F or above with the time
test.why: Only an internal temperature reading is evidence of safety.

test.q: Dinner ended at 8:30; the chicken came out at 5:50. What happens to leftovers?
choices: Discard them; they were out more than two hours
Reheat them to 165 °F and keep them
test.why: The two-hour rule counts from when the food left the oven.

test.q: Which is the strongest reflection statement?
choices: Tape the seam guide on before the first seam, because the untaped seam ran 1/8 inch off; see photo 3
test.why: Action, reason and evidence make a change that a reader can check.

write.prompt: Choose a project: a two-course meal for eight or a simple sewn piece. Write the specification, a cost sheet with at least eight line items at unit prices (labeled example), a timeline built backwards from the deadline with two checkpoints, and a safety page. Then explain why each part is there and what would go wrong without it.
tips: Write every spec line so it can be checked with a tool: a cup, a scale, a tape measure, a clock.
Compute each cost line as unit price times amount, add a cushion, and compare the total to your budget.
Start the timeline at the deadline and step backwards; put thawing and cooling days ahead.
Copy the standard safety figures exactly: poultry 165 °F, ground meat 160 °F, hold hot above 140 °F, fridge at or below 40 °F.
Name the one thing most likely to go wrong and the checkpoint that would catch it.
